clue.text: Red flag I unfurled for President

indicators.note: a flag unfurled is shaken loose and spread out, so these letters are spread into a new order

explanation.surface: A red banner shaken out to greet a head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfurled' rearranges the letters of RED FLAG I. James Garfield was the 20th US President.
explanation.definitionFit: James Garfield was a nineteenth-century American head of state, so a specific example of the defining word.

clue.text: One used to select neutral clothing last

parts.note: gear is informal for clothing
to last is to stick, or keep going

explanation.surface: Someone picks plain clothes that will wear well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neutral' suggests beige clothes but is the car's neutral gear; 'last' is the verb, endure.
explanation.definitionFit: The lever in a manual car is moved to choose a gear, including the neutral position.

clue.text: From memory, a fancy fellow comes fast

parts.note: RAM is computer memory, random access memory
Dan was an old title for a master, as in Dan Cupid, the god of fancy or love

explanation.surface: A dandy says from memory that he is coming quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' looks like speed but is the Muslim holy month of fasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramadan is the month in which Muslims abstain from food during daylight, a religious period of fasting.

clue.text: Crack that's not got beyond a cirole?

definitions.text: Crack that's not got beyond a cirole?

parts.words: Crack that's not got beyond a cirole
parts.note: a wisecrack only understood within a small group of insiders, not by anyone outside it

explanation.surface: A gap that hasn't spread past a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The paper prints 'cirole', a misprint for 'circle'. 'Crack' is a joke, and 'not got' means not understood: only the circle gets it.
explanation.definitionFit: A private joke shared by a clique is understood only by its members, outsiders not getting it.

clue.text: Racecourse winner's drawn out first

indicators.note: first places the drawn-out piece ahead of the winner

parts.note: long means drawn out, protracted
a champ is a champion, a winner

explanation.surface: The winning horse is pulled out first at the track.
explanation.walkthrough: Longchamp is the Paris racecourse that stages the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe.
explanation.definitionFit: Longchamp is a famous horse-racing venue in the Bois de Boulogne, Paris.

clue.text: Wine-merchant's opening branches for Christmas in every area

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, taken here from the merchant

parts.note: holly sprigs are the traditional evergreen decoration hung at Christmas

explanation.surface: A vintner's shop opens, decked out with festive greenery in every corner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening' takes the first letter W of Wine-merchant's.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in every area is done completely, the adverb meaning totally or entirely.

clue.text: Fancy eating batter and cream!

indicators.note: eating puts one piece inside another, as food goes in a mouth

parts.note: to fancy is to wish for
to batter is to hit

explanation.surface: Desire for pancake mix and cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'batter' is a pancake mix in the surface but the verb HIT here; 'eating' puts it inside WISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Cream as a colour is a pale off-white shade, the adjective in both cases.

clue.text: Beat poor Rosy for going out a lot

parts.note: to beat someone is to outdo them

indicators.note: poor signals that the letters of Rosy are in bad shape and rearranged

explanation.surface: Outperform unfortunate Rosy, who loves nights out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges ROSY into ORSY. 'going out' means outside in the open air, not socialising.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoorsy person loves fresh air and spends a lot of time outside.

clue.text: Female sound coming from toilet block

indicators.note: sound coming from signals a word said aloud rather than spelt

parts.note: a loo is a toilet and a cell is a block or unit

explanation.surface: A noise emanates from the public lavatories.
explanation.walkthrough: LOO CELL said aloud gives the woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucille is a woman's given name, so it stands for a female.

clue.text: Main roads converge from East and West End

parts.note: the A1 and the M1 are the two great trunk roads north out of London
the second main road, the M1, met from the east

explanation.surface: Two trunk roads meet from opposite directions at the end of the line.
explanation.walkthrough: Write A1 heading east and M1 heading west so they meet: A1 plus 1M share the figure 1, read as the letter I, giving A-I-M. 'converge from East and West' describes that meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: An aim is an end or purpose, the goal one is striving towards.

clue.text: Judge in bar is one caught waving flag

indicators.note: IS goes inside the bar, the clue saying is sits in it

parts.note: an ingot is a bar of cast metal, typically gold
the Roman numeral I stands for one
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A magistrate in a pub, caught brandishing a banner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' looks like a pub but is a gold INGOT; 'in' puts IS inside it to give INGOIST.
explanation.definitionFit: Jingoism is aggressive patriotism, and flag-waving is the idiom for that zealous display of national pride.

clue.text: Party hack becoming personal assistant

parts.note: a side is a party or faction in a dispute
to hack in football is to kick an opponent's shins

explanation.surface: A party writer is promoted to be someone's aide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hack' suggests a journalist, but it is the footballing sense, a kick.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidekick is a close helper or companion, informally someone's assistant.

clue.text: Admission by pilot about possible expression of wish

indicators.note: the pilot's admission is placed about, that is around, the other piece

parts.note: a pilot might admit 'I fly'
on means feasible, as in 'that's not on'

explanation.surface: An airman's confession about what he might hope for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts ON inside I FLY.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase introduces a wistful longing, as in saying you wish something were so.

clue.text: Bars wingers from Italian team holding hands

indicators.note: wingers play on the flanks, so these are the outer letters of the word

parts.note: at bridge North and South are partners, a team holding two of the four hands

explanation.surface: Footballers from an Italian side are pictured arm in arm in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wingers from' takes the first and last letters of Italian, I and N. In bridge North and South play as partners, so the team holding those hands is NS.
explanation.definitionFit: Inns are pubs or taverns, and a bar is likewise a place serving drink, so these are synonyms.

clue.text: What's a bug just upset? Point to cow

indicators.note: upset knocks these letters over into a new order

parts.note: E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Asking what has made an insect upset, pointing at a cow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges A BUG JUST into SUBJUGAT; 'cow' is the verb, intimidate.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow someone is to intimidate them into submission, to bring them under control.

clue.text: Corner boy satisfied with plum draw

definitions.text: Corner boy satisfied with plum draw

parts.words: Corner boy satisfied with plum draw
parts.note: evokes the nursery-rhyme lad sitting in a corner who pulled out a plum from his pie and was pleased with himself

explanation.surface: A lad loitering on a corner is pleased with a lucky draw.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme the boy sat in a corner, put in his thumb, pulled out a plum and said 'What a good boy am I'.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme character sat in a corner and was delighted with the plum he drew out of his Christmas pie.

clue.text: One getting peckish on the job

definitions.text: One getting peckish on the job

parts.words: One getting peckish on the job
parts.note: peckish suggests hungry but here means giving pecks, kisses, as one's work

explanation.surface: A worker who gets hungry while working.
explanation.walkthrough: A kissogram is a messenger who delivers a greeting with a kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: A kissogram performer delivers kisses (pecks) as a paid novelty greeting, so pecking is the job.

clue.text: Opera part is thought to restrict performer

indicators.note: the clue words restrict, or enclose, the answer within them

explanation.surface: A role in an opera is believed to limit a singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restrict' signals the answer held inside the run of letters in opeRA PART IS Thought.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapper is a musician who performs rhythmic spoken lyrics, a kind of entertainer.

clue.text: She parks by building way across the mountains

indicators.note: building assembles these letters into a new structure

explanation.surface: A woman parks beside a building site on a mountain road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'building' rearranges SHE PARKS BY. The Khyber Pass links Afghanistan and Pakistan.
explanation.definitionFit: The Khyber Pass is a famous route over the mountains between Afghanistan and Pakistan.

clue.text: Semi cut short when one's netted for Town

indicators.note: netted means caught inside, as a fish in a net

parts.note: semi is a prefix meaning half
the Roman numeral I stands for one

indicators.note: short means the last letter is lopped off

parts.note: to axe is to cut

explanation.surface: A semi-detached house is cut back while a resident is caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'netted' puts I inside HALF; 'short' trims AXE to AX. Halifax is a town in West Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Halifax is a West Yorkshire town, so a specific example of an urban settlement.

clue.text: Teeth disposed to chatter

indicators.note: disposed means arranged, so the letters are set out anew

explanation.surface: Teeth inclined to clatter together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disposed' rearranges CHATTER. A ratchet is a toothed wheel or bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratchet is a mechanism of angled teeth engaged by a pawl, so it is essentially a set of teeth.

clue.text: Difficult March ends in delay to farm crop

indicators.note: the ends of the four words supply their last letters in turn

explanation.surface: A tough March means late harvests on the farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ends in' takes the last letters of delay, to, farm and crop. To yomp is military slang for a gruelling march with full kit.
explanation.definitionFit: Yomping is the Royal Marines' term for marching laboriously over rough terrain with a heavy load.

clue.text: Officer: outstanding American army swimmer

parts.note: OC is an officer commanding
top means first-rate or outstanding

explanation.surface: An excellent American army officer who swims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'army' is a pun on 'arm-y': the creature has many arms.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea creature has eight arms and swims, so it is a many-armed swimmer.

clue.text: European bringing periodical raising of hope?

parts.note: a mag, short for magazine, is a periodical

indicators.note: raising lifts the word up, reading it backwards in a down clue

parts.note: a ray of hope is a glimmer of it, so ray stands for hope

explanation.surface: A magazine that brings optimism to a continental reader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raising of' reverses RAY to YAR in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A Magyar is a Hungarian, a native of a Central European country.

clue.text: Nations coming together in uniform parade

indicators.note: the nations piece sits in the uniform piece

parts.note: flat means uniform or even, as in a flat rate
the UN is the United Nations

explanation.surface: Countries gather in military dress for a march past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uniform' looks like clothing but means FLAT; 'in' puts UN inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To flaunt is to parade or show off ostentatiously, a verb in both cases.

clue.text: Who cares about dull drama queen?

indicators.note: the drama and the queen go about, that is around, dull

parts.note: No (or Noh) is classical Japanese drama
ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the Queen
matt means dull, without shine

explanation.surface: Who is bothered about a boring diva?
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts MATT inside NO + ER.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a shrug of indifference, said when it makes no difference, just like 'who cares?'

clue.text: Show-off imparting instant torment

parts.note: a flash is an instant, as in 'in a flash'
to harry is to harass or torment

explanation.surface: An exhibitionist dishing out sudden misery.
explanation.walkthrough: A Flash Harry is British slang for a flashy, ostentatious man.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a brash, ostentatious man who likes to flaunt himself, a typical exhibitionist.

clue.text: Page greeting exotic character

parts.note: hi is an informal greeting

explanation.surface: A page boy welcomes a strange figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' is a letter; this one is from the Greek alphabet, hence exotic.
explanation.definitionFit: The twenty-first letter of the Greek alphabet is a foreign written symbol, hence an exotic letter.

clue.text: Exercise with Penny in the buff

indicators.note: the penny goes in the exercise piece

parts.note: to exercise strength is to exert it

explanation.surface: Working out naked with a woman called Penny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the buff' suggests nakedness, but 'in' places P inside EXERT and 'buff' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A buff is an enthusiast who knows a lot about a subject, so a knowledgeable specialist.

clue.text: Trendy folk backing experiment on sheep farm?

indicators.note: backing means the experiment and the sheep are read backwards as one run

parts.note: a test is an experiment
rams are male sheep

explanation.surface: Fashionable people supporting research at a sheep farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' reads TEST RAMS backwards; the farm and the question mark set the scene for testing on sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: The smart set is a fashionable social clique, the trendy, stylish people of the day.
